lines.text: Your phone is listening to you.
lines.see: Tight on a phone face up on a dark table, amber sound rings drift into its microphone, an ad card pops up above it

lines.text: At least, that's what one marketing company told advertisers.
lines.see: Crane up and back: the phone shrinks, a giant glowing pitch-deck slide rises out of the dark above the table

lines.text: Cox Media Group called it Active Listening: ads based on what you say near your phone.
lines.see: Push into the slide: ACTIVE LISTENING, a microphone icon, voice waves turning into ad cards that fly out to a wall of phones

lines.text: Here's the weird part. Google dropped them from its partner programme.
lines.see: Three partner badges orbit the slide; one goes dark and falls away into the fog

lines.text: And Meta said it doesn't use your microphone for ads.
lines.see: Close on the phone's microphone grille: it stays dark grey, a second badge dims

lines.text: Then America's consumer watchdog, the FTC, looked inside.
lines.see: Camera flies through the slide's surface, the slide turns to gold line-art as we pass through it

lines.text: It never listened. It was resold email lists from data brokers.
lines.see: Behind the slide: no microphones, just data-broker towers pumping streams of amber envelopes into the deck

lines.text: Three firms paid $930,000 for a microphone that didn't exist.
lines.see: Headline $930,000 counts up, the envelope streams cut off, the slide flickers out

lines.text: Researchers tested over 17,000 Android apps. Not one switched on the mic.
lines.see: Power-of-ten pull out to a field of 17,000 app tiles, an amber scan wave rolls across, every mic stays dark

lines.text: It doesn't need to hear you. It has your location, your searches, your friends.
lines.see: Dive back down to the phone: a city map under the table, location pins, search bars and friends' phones send amber trails into it

lines.text: So, creepy coincidence, or something worse than listening?
lines.see: Back to the same phone on the table (loop to frame 0), the ad card pops, question headline, comment bubble

facts.claim: 404 Media reported that a Cox Media Group (CMG) marketing unit claimed it could target ads using 'Active Listening': what people say near device microphones
404 Media obtained a CMG pitch deck for Active Listening; after 404 Media asked for comment, Google removed CMG from its advertising Partners Program
Meta: 'Meta does not use your phone's microphone for ads and we've been public about this for years'; Amazon Ads said it has never worked with CMG on this program
Facebook newsroom, 2 June 2016: Facebook does not use your phone's microphone to inform ads or to change what you see in News Feed

FTC: the service 'did not, in fact, listen in on consumers' conversations or use voice data at all'; it 'consisted of reselling, at a significant markup, email lists obtained from other data brokers'. CMG pays $880,000, MindSift and 1010 Digital Works $25,000 each, $930,000 in total
FTC finalised the orders against CMG and the two other firms
Northeastern University researchers tested more than 17,000 popular Android apps: 'not a single app activated the microphone'; some apps sent screenshots and screen video to third parties instead
Ad tracking works from web searches, social media activity and connections (who you know), not eavesdropping (David Choffnes, Northeastern)

publish.title: Is your phone listening to you? #shorts
publish.caption:
A marketing firm told advertisers it could target ads from what you say near your phone. In 2026 the FTC said it never listened at all: it was resold email lists. Your phone doesn't need your voice. It already has your location, your searches and your friends.

Creepy coincidence or worse? 👇
